chapters.title: The Jubilee: God's Great Reset
chapters.subtitle: Every fiftieth year: debts released, servants freed, families home, land at rest
chapters.nutshell: Leviticus 25 commands a fiftieth year, the jubilee, announced by the ram's horn on the Day of Atonement. Israelites in debt-servitude went free, family land returned to its original owners, and the land rested. Behind it stands God's claim: “the land is mine” and “they are my servants whom I brought out of Egypt”, so no family could be poor or owned for ever.
chapters.bigIdea: The jubilee built release, return and rest into Israel's calendar, because the land and the people belong to God, not to the powerful.

sections.h: What the text says: the words
p: The jubilee is the *yovel*, the “ram's horn” blown to announce it (Lev 25:9–10). Latin turned it into *iubilaeus*, and it was easily linked with *iubilare*, “to shout for joy”, a happy accident of sound rather than the Hebrew meaning. The key command is to proclaim *deror*, “release” or “liberty” (25:10). Its partner is *shemittah*, the “release” of debts in the seventh year (Deut 15:1–2), and *ge'ullah*, “redemption”, the right to buy back family land (Lev 25:24) through a *go'el*, a kinsman-redeemer (25:25, 47–49).

sections.h: What the text says: the fiftieth year
p: Israel counted seven Sabbath years, seven times seven, forty-nine years. Then on the Day of Atonement, the tenth day of the seventh month, the shofar sounded through the land and the fiftieth year was made holy (Lev 25:8–10). Whether the fiftieth year was also the first year of the next cycle is debated. Release began on the day of cleansing.

In that year “each of you shall return to his property and each of you to his clan” (25:10, 13). Israelites who had sold themselves for debt went free with their children (25:39–41, 54). The land was not sown or reaped (25:11–12), and God promised a harvest in the sixth year big enough for three years (25:20–22). A sale of land was really a lease of its harvests until the jubilee, priced by the years left: “you shall not wrong one another” (25:14–17). Houses in walled cities were an exception (25:29–30), and the Levites kept special rights (25:32–34).

Two sentences explain the whole law. “The land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me” (25:23). And “they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt; they shall not be sold as slaves” (25:42, 55). Because God owns the land and has freed the people, no Israelite could own another for ever, and no family could lose its inheritance for ever.

Deuteronomy dreams that “there will be no poor among you” (15:4), yet commands, “you shall open wide your hand” (15:7–11). The jubilee capped poverty at one lifetime. It restored dignity, family, land and rest, and showed God as owner, redeemer and liberator.

The Hebrew Bible never clearly records a jubilee being celebrated, and scholars debate whether it was ever practised in full. We do see the idea at work. Under King Zedekiah the people proclaimed *deror* and freed their Hebrew slaves, then took them back; God answered, “I proclaim to you liberty… to the sword” (Jer 34:8–22). The exile let the land “enjoy its Sabbaths” for seventy years (2 Chr 36:21). After the return Nehemiah made the nobles give back fields and stop charging interest (Neh 5), and the people promised to keep the Sabbath year (10:31). Ezekiel speaks of “the year of liberty” (46:17), and Isaiah 61 takes up the jubilee as a hope.

Ancient kings in Mesopotamia sometimes issued *andurāru* edicts, royal releases of debts, such as the edict of Ammi-saduqa of Babylon (around 1646 BC, dates vary). Israel's release differed: it stood on a fixed calendar in God's law, not on a new king's goodwill.

The rabbis taught that the jubilee lapsed when the tribes east of the Jordan were exiled, since it applied only when all Israel lived in the land (Talmud Arakhin 32b, as usually cited). The Sabbath-year release of debts continued, but people stopped lending before it. Hillel (1st century BC) created the *prozbul*, a court document that let a loan survive the seventh year, so the poor could still borrow (Mishnah Shevi'it 10:3–4). In modern Israel the Sabbath year of the land is still observed in various ways, including the debated *heter mechira*, a sale of land to a non-Jew for the year.

Leviticus 25:10 is cast on the Liberty Bell in Philadelphia (18th century), a verse later taken up by those working to end slavery. Since 1300 the Catholic Church has proclaimed holy “jubilee” years, and around the year 2000 a worldwide movement called for the debts of the poorest nations to be cancelled.

The jubilee asks what we hold as if we owned it for ever. Our time, money, land and even other people's debts to us belong to God. It invites us to release grudges and debts, to give rest to ourselves and to those who work for us, and to help families out of poverty that traps one generation after another. Its links with forgiveness and the gospel are traced in the next chapter.

chapters.title: Jubilee and the Gospel: the Year of the Lord's Favour
chapters.subtitle: From Leviticus 25 to Isaiah 61, Luke 4 and the restoration of all things
chapters.nutshell: Isaiah 61 pictures an anointed one proclaiming a jubilee: liberty to captives and “the year of the LORD's favour”. Jesus read it in Nazareth and said, “Today this Scripture is fulfilled.” The Greek word for jubilee release, *aphesis*, is the same word the New Testament uses for forgiveness, so the gospel can be heard as God's great jubilee.
chapters.bigIdea: In Jesus, God proclaims a jubilee: release from debt, bondage and sin, and a homecoming for his people and his whole creation.
skeleton: Isaiah 61: the anointed one proclaims a jubilee
Aphesis: release and forgiveness are one word
Jubilee in the Gospels and Acts
Creation set free and all things restored

p: “The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me to bring good news to the poor… to proclaim liberty to the captives… to proclaim the year of the LORD's favour” (Isa 61:1–2). The word for liberty is *deror*, the jubilee word of Leviticus 25:10. The speaker is anointed (*mashach*, from which comes *mashiach*, Messiah) to announce a jubilee. Isaiah 58:6 adds the call “to let the oppressed go free”.

sections.h: What the text says: Jesus in Nazareth
p: In the synagogue at Nazareth Jesus read Isaiah 61:1–2, with a line from 58:6, and stopped before “the day of vengeance of our God”. Then he sat down and said, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:16–21). His first public sermon in Luke is the announcement of a jubilee (see the chapter on preaching).

In the Greek Bible the jubilee and Sabbath-year release are called *aphesis* (Lev 25:10; Deut 15:1–2), and Isaiah's *deror* is *aphesis* too. Luke 4:18 uses it twice: *aphesis* for the captives and sending the oppressed away *en aphesei*, “in release”. The same word means “forgiveness” in Matthew 26:28, Luke 24:47, Acts 2:38, Ephesians 1:7 and Colossians 1:14. Forgiveness in the gospel is a jubilee release, a debt cancelled, not a debt paid.

sections.h: Jewish background: the Day of Atonement and 11QMelchizedek
p: The jubilee was announced on the Day of Atonement: release flowed from cleansing. A Dead Sea Scroll, 11QMelchizedek, reads Leviticus 25, Deuteronomy 15 and Isaiah 61 together. It pictures a heavenly deliverer, Melchizedek, who proclaims release to the captives and atonement for their sins on the Day of Atonement at the end of the tenth jubilee. This shows that some Jews before Jesus already read Isaiah 61 as a jubilee of the last days. Some scholars also suggest Jesus began his ministry in a Sabbath or jubilee year; the dating is uncertain.

sections.h: New Testament: jubilee in the Gospels and Acts
p: Jesus taught his disciples to pray, “forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors” (Matt 6:12), jubilee language in the Lord's Prayer. His parable of the unforgiving servant turns on a huge debt released and a small one not released (Matt 18:23–35). Zacchaeus gave half his goods to the poor and restored fourfold, and Jesus said, “Today salvation has come to this house” (Luke 19:8–9).

The first believers shared their goods, and “there was not a needy person among them” (Acts 4:34), words widely noted as an echo of Deuteronomy 15:4. Peter spoke of “the times of restoration of all things” (Acts 3:21).

sections.h: The heart of God: release, return and rest
p: Through a Jewish lens the jubilee reveals God's heart. He hears the cry of slaves (Ex 3:7–8). He owns the land, so he will not allow his people to lose their inheritance for ever. He builds rest and return into time itself. So salvation is not only escape from the world but homecoming and restoration.

Creation itself will be “set free from its bondage to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom 8:19–23): the land's rest becomes creation's release. “There remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Heb 4:9), and in the new Jerusalem God dwells with his people (Rev 21–22). Many Christians also read the *go'el*, the kinsman-redeemer like Boaz, as a picture of the Messiah who redeems his family; this is a typological reading.

Living the jubilee means releasing debts and grudges as we have been released; resting from anxious striving and keeping Sabbath rhythms; giving generously so that no one among us is in need; and working to free people from cycles of poverty and shame. Every act of forgiveness is a small jubilee and a foretaste of the restoration of all things.

keyPoints: Isaiah 61 uses the jubilee word *deror*: an anointed one proclaims release and the year of the LORD's favour.
Jesus read Isaiah 61 in Nazareth and said it was fulfilled that day.
*Aphesis*, the Greek word for jubilee release, is the New Testament word for forgiveness.

The jubilee hope reaches its goal in the restoration of all things and creation set free.
